rows.selection_reason: No experiments have been completed, so the primary uncertainty is what the baseline performance looks like and which modality/architecture choices matter. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest, most standard configuration in the space: it uses a well-understood linear encoder (PCA), the simplest profile setting, and isolates the RNA signal without confounding from image features, complex aggregation, or fusion. Establishing this baseline is essential before interpreting any multimodal or image-only result, because it tells us (a) how much signal RNA alone carries, (b) the performance floor, and (c) how much headroom exists for the image modality or more complex architectures to exploit. Under a limited budget, this single experiment reduces the most uncertainty per trial by anchoring the entire comparison space.

The sole completed experiment (config_001, rna_only/singleprofile/pca_n2000) yields a low accuracy of 0.485, leaving substantial uncertainty about where the performance bottleneck lies. The most fundamental open question for a multimodal cellular profiling study is whether the image modality carries any independent predictive signal. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) cleanly tests this by isolating the image channel with a standard, well-understood encoder while removing RNA entirely. If image_only performs well, it confirms the image modality is informative and justifies investing subsequent experiments in multimodal fusion strategies. If it performs poorly, it indicates the image channel needs a stronger encoder (e.g., ViT) or that signal is primarily in the RNA modality, redirecting effort toward better RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt). This experiment maximizes information per trial because the answer bifurcates the entire search strategy: it determines whether to prioritize multimodal configurations or RNA-encoder improvements in the remaining budget.

Evidence: RNA (PCA n2000, singleprofile) achieves 0.485 accuracy while image (ResNet50, singleprofile) achieves only 0.208—near chance level. This large gap raises a critical strategic question: is the image modality fundamentally uninformative for this task, or does it simply need a stronger encoder? This experiment (image_only, singleprofile, ViT-L) directly tests that question by changing only the encoder relative to config_010, keeping profile setting constant for a clean comparison. If ViT-L substantially improves over ResNet50, it validates the image modality and justifies investing in multimodal fusion experiments; if it remains poor, we can confidently deprioritize all ~36 multimodal configurations and focus remaining budget on RNA encoder/aggregation optimization. With only 2 experiments completed, resolving whether image is viable at all is the highest-information decision that shapes the entire subsequent search strategy.

Evidence: RNA-only with pca_n2000 (config_001) achieves 0.485 acc, far exceeding both image-only baselines (~0.21-0.23), establishing RNA as the dominant modality. However, we have only tested one RNA encoder (pca_n2000, a linear projection). Uncertainty: whether a learned non-linear encoder (scvi_n200) captures richer single-cell structure that translates to better classification. This experiment (config_004: rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_001, isolating the RNA encoder choice while holding profile setting constant. It is the best use of the next budget slot because (1) it directly tests whether encoder sophistication matters before investing in more complex multimodal or multiprofile configurations, (2) a positive result would justify exploring scvi_n200 in multimodal settings, while a null result would confirm pca_n2000 is sufficient and redirect effort toward profile aggregation or fusion strategies, and (3) it reduces uncertainty on a foundational design axis that underlies many downstream configuration choices.

Evidence: RNA-only models (pca_n2000: 0.485, scvi_n200: 0.520) substantially outperform image-only models (resnet50: 0.208, ViT-L: 0.227), establishing RNA as the dominant signal. However, image performance is only slightly above chance, leaving genuine uncertainty about whether image features provide complementary information in a fused setting or merely add noise. Question tested: Does combining the best RNA encoder (scvi_n200) with the best image encoder (ViT-L) via simple concatenation in a singleprofile setting yield any gain over the RNA-only baseline of 0.520? This is the cleanest multimodal test—singleprofile minimizes confounding variables, and concat is the simplest fusion. Why best next experiment: Resolving whether multimodal fusion is viable at all is the highest-leverage structural decision. A positive result validates ~36 multimodal configurations for further exploration; a null or negative result efficiently prunes that entire branch, redirecting budget toward RNA-only multiprofile/aggregation and encoder choices where the signal clearly resides.

Evidence: RNA encoders (scvi_n200 at 0.520, pca_n2000 at 0.485) dominate over image-only models (~0.21-0.23), and the best result so far (config_034, multimodal scvi_n200+ViT concat) is only marginally above RNA-only scvi_n200. The multiprofile dimension is completely untested across all 5 completed experiments, representing the largest source of uncertainty in the design space. Question: config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) directly compares against config_004 (same RNA encoder, singleprofile) to isolate whether aggregating multiple profiles improves the dominant RNA signal, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool) as a conservative first probe. Why this is the best next experiment: Since RNA carries most of the predictive signal, establishing whether multiprofile helps at the RNA level before committing to more complex multimodal-multiprofile configurations (which confound profile-setting, aggregation, and fusion effects) is the most information-efficient use of the next budget slot. A positive result would justify investing in multimodal multiprofile variants (e.g., config_036/038); a null result would redirect effort toward fusion strategies or alternative encoders.

Evidence: config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) achieved 0.650 acc / 0.628 F1, a dramatic ~13-point gain over its singleprofile counterpart (config_004, 0.520). This makes multiprofile + scvi_n200 the clearly dominant direction. However, we have only tested one aggregation strategy (avgpool) for this setting. The aggregation method is the critical mechanism that determines how multiple profiles are combined, and transformer-based aggregation could capture inter-profile relationships that simple averaging discards. Question: Does transformer aggregation outperform avgpool for multiprofile scvi_n200, and if so, by how much? Why this is the best next experiment: It is the most direct exploitation of our strongest result while resolving a high-uncertainty design choice (aggregation) that could meaningfully shift performance. A large gap would justify further transformer-based multimodal experiments; a small gap would confirm avgpool sufficiency and redirect budget toward other levers (e.g., adding image in multiprofile mode). Under a limited budget, clarifying this binary choice before branching into multimodal multiprofile variants is the most information-efficient use of the next run.

Evidence: Multiprofile RNA (scvi_n200) is the strongest configuration found so far (acc ~0.65), while image-only models are very weak (acc ~0.21-0.23). The only multimodal test (config_034, singleprofile) showed only a marginal gain over RNA-only (0.532 vs 0.520), suggesting image adds little in singleprofile mode. Critical uncertainty: does the multiprofile setting—which unlocked a ~13% gain for RNA alone—also unlock complementary signal from the image modality? This experiment (config_038: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) directly tests whether the best RNA encoder combined with the best image encoder in a multiprofile multimodal setting can exceed the 0.653 RNA-only ceiling. It uses transformer aggregation (marginally better than avgpool in config_006) and concat fusion (the only fusion tested in config_034). If it beats 0.653, image is a useful complement in the richer profile space; if it does not, we can confidently deprioritize all remaining multimodal and image-only configurations, saving budget for RNA-encoder exploration (e.g., scgpt).

The current best configuration (config_038: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) achieves 0.721 accuracy. The most significant unexplored design dimension is the RNA encoder choice: we have evidence that scvi_n200 > pca_n2000, but scgpt has never been tested. Config_050 isolates this single variable by swapping scvi_n200 → scgpt while keeping all other settings identical to the best config. This directly answers whether a generative-model-based encoder (scGPT) can outperform the VAE-based encoder (scVI) in the highest-performing multimodal regime. Under a limited budget, resolving this major architectural question is more informative than testing minor variations (e.g., concat vs. weighted fusion) on an already-validated encoder, because a positive result would open an entirely new optimization direction, while a negative result would confirm scvi_n200 as the correct choice and focus remaining budget on fusion/aggregation refinements.

Evidence: config_038 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) is the clear best at 0.7207 acc / 0.6815 F1, and all its individual components (scvi_n200 over pca_n2000, multiprofile over singleprofile, transformer over avgpool, imagenet_vit_l over resnet50, multimodal over unimodal) are supported by prior experiments. However, the fusion strategy has only been tested as 'concat' in this top-performing regime. Question: config_039 changes only the fusion from concat to weighted, directly testing whether learned modality weighting can further improve over a fixed concatenation in the best-known setting. Rationale: This is the highest-value exploitation step—every other hyperparameter is already at its empirically best value, so isolating the fusion choice gives a clean read on whether this design axis still has headroom. If weighted fusion helps, it identifies a new improvement direction; if it does not, it confirms concat is sufficient and redirects budget toward other untested axes (e.g., alternative image encoders or profile counts). Under a limited budget, this single-variable change from the current best is the most informative next experiment.
